label: theorem: eeroklas
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{theorem: eeroklas}
    Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a small permutation class. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Then there exists a regular language $L_{\mathcal{F}}$ and a length-preserving bijection
        \[f_{\mathcal{F}}: L_{\mathcal{F}} \rightarrow \mathcal{F}\]
        satisfying the following property: for every first-order logic sentence $\Psi$ on $\mathcal{F}$ there exists a first-order logic  sentence $\Phi$ on $L_{\mathcal{F}}$ so that 
        \[\{w \in L_\mathcal{F}: w \models \Phi\} = \{w \in L_\mathcal{F}: f_\mathcal{F}(w) \models \Psi\}.\]
        The same conclusion also holds for sentences in monadic second-order logic.
        \item{(sketched)} The bijection $f_\mathcal{F}$ is in fact a monadic second-order isomorphism: that is, for every sentence $\Phi$ in monadic second-order logic on $L_\mathcal{F}$ there exists a corresponding sentence in monadic second-order logic on $\mathcal{F}$ for which the conclusion above holds. In addition, it is also possible to construct a regular language $L_\mathcal{F}'$ and a length-preserving bijection $f'_\mathcal{F}: L_\mathcal{F}' \rightarrow \mathcal{F}$ which is a first-order isomorphism. 
        \item For the last three assertions, suppose that $\mathcal{F}$ is not finite. There exist a positive real number $\alpha$, a real number $\beta \geq 1$, and a non-negative integer $c$ so that 
        \[\vert \mathcal{F}_n\vert = (\alpha+o(1))\cdot \beta ^n\cdot n^c.\]
        \item Given a monadic second-order sentence $\Psi$ on $\mathcal{F}$, write \[\mathcal{F}^\Psi_n := \{\sigma \in \mathcal{F}_n: \sigma \models \Psi\}.\]
        Then the sets $\mathcal{F}^\Psi_n$ have a rational generating function.
        \item For every first-order $\mathrm{TOTO}$ sentence $\Phi$ the limit  $\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \mathbb{P} (\pi \models \Phi)$ exists, where $\pi$  is taken uniformly at random from $\mathcal{F}_n$. 
    \end{enumerate}

label: claim: I,D decomposes properly
title: \protect\claimname
body_md:
\label{claim: I,D decomposes properly}
    For each $s$, the sub-word $u^{(s)}$ satisfies the conditions~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 1} and~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 2}. In particular, the word $w$ can be expressed as a concatenation $w = u_1\dots u_\ell$ for some $u_1,\dots,u_\ell$ chosen so that for every $j$ we have $u_j = u^{(s_j)}$ for some $s_j$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given an index $s$, we start with the case when $i(s) = j(s) = s$. In this case, we must have $w \models \psi_{=}(i(s),j(s))$, which in turn implies that $\rho_4(w_{i(s)}) = \{L,R\}$. Thus, the word $u^{(s)}$ that  consists of a single letter $w_{i(s)}$ trivially satisfies both of the conditions~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 1} and~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 2}. 

    Now suppose that $i(s) \neq j(s)$, and thus we must have $i(s) < j(s)$.  Thus the fourth line ensures that $w \models \forall t: \psi_{\neq}(i(s),j(s),t)$, which by construction of $\psi_{\neq}$ implies
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] $\rho_4(w_{i(s)}) = \{L\}$,
        \item[(ii)] $\rho_4(w_{j(s)}) = \{R\}$, and 
        \item[(iii)] $\rho_4(w_t) = \emptyset$ for every $i(s) < t < j(s)$. 
    \end{enumerate}
    These conditions together are clearly equivalent to the fact that $u^{(s)}$ satisfies both of the conditions~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 1} and~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 2}, which proves the first part of the claim. 

    To prove the second part, observe that the sub-words $u^{(s)}$ cover $w$ as each $w_s$ is trivially contained in $u^{(s)}$. In addition, recall that each $u^{(s)}$ consists of a set of contiguous letters. Hence, it suffices to prove that for each $s \neq s'$, the sub-words $u^{(s)}$ and $u^{(s')}$ are either identical or disjoint. 

    Suppose that $s \neq s'$ are chosen so that $u^{(s)}$ and $u^{(s')}$ are neither identical nor disjoint. Since both of them consists of a contiguous set of letters, we must have $i(s) \in [i(s'),j(s')]$ or $i(s')\in [i(s),j(s)]$. By symmetry, we may assume that the first case occurs. 

    Since $u^{(s')}$ satisfies property~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 1} and $L \in \rho_4(w_{i(s)})$, we must have $i(s) = i(s')$. As $u^{(s)}$ and $u^{(s')}$ are not identical, we must have $j(s) \neq j(s')$, and by symmetry, we may assume that $j(s) < j(s')$. Since $R \in \rho_4(w_{j(s)})$ and $j(s) \in [i(s),j(s')]$ this contradicts the fact that $u^{(s')}$ satisfies property~\eqref{eq: consistent conditions for I,D - 2}. This completes the proof of Claim~\ref{claim: I,D decomposes properly}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_L$ so that $\mathcal{F} = \bigcap_{i=1}^{L} \mathrm{Av}(\varphi_i)$.  For each $i \in [L]$, let $A_i(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2)$ denote the first-order formula given by 
    \begin{align*}
     \exists z_1,\dots,z_{|\varphi_i|} :& \bigwedge_{j=1}^{|\varphi_i|} \left(z_j \in [x_1,y_1]_1 \times [x_2,y_2]_2\right)\\
    & \land \bigwedge_{j = 1}^{|\varphi_i| - 1} \bigwedge_{\ell =  j + 1}^{|\varphi_i|} \left(z_j <_1 z_\ell \land \left(z_j <_2 z_\ell \iff \varphi_i(j) < \varphi_i(\ell)\right)\right),
    \end{align*}
    and set 
    \[\upsilon_{\mathcal{F}}(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2) := \bigwedge_{i=1}^{L} \left(\neg A_i(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2)\right).\]

    To check that $\upsilon_\mathcal{F}(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2)$ satisfies the required properties, suppose that we have $\sigma \models A_i(a_1,a_2,b_1,b_2)$  for some $i$. The top line of $A_i$ implies that each of the points $z_1,\dots,z_{|\varphi_i|}$ is contained in $[a_1,b_1]_1 \times [a_2,b_2]_2$, while the second line implies that they form a sub-permutation that coincides with $\varphi_i$. Thus we have $\sigma \models \upsilon_{\mathcal{F}}(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2)$ if and only if the sub-permutation $\tau$ of $\sigma$ consisting of the points in $[x_1,y_1]_1 \times [x_2,y_2]_2$ does not contain $\varphi_i$ as a sub-permutation for any $1 \leq i \leq L$, as required. The second part of the statement follows by defining $A_i$ to be the first-order sentence obtained from $A_i(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2)$ by deleting the second part of the top line, and setting $\hat{\upsilon}_\mathcal{F} := \bigwedge_{i=1}^L \left(\neg A_i\right)$.

We construct the sentences $\Delta_d$ by induction. As the base

For each $\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_k$, let $\Delta_{\tau,d}$ denote the first-order sentence obtained by applying Lemma~\ref{lemma: handling Q_ks for bijection} with $\hat\Delta:=\Delta_{d-1}$, and attaching $\exists$-quantifier with every free variable. 

    To handle with words whose profile is $\mathrm{inc}$ or $\mathrm{dec}$, we let $\delta(x,y)$ be the formula
    \begin{align*}
        x\leq y\ \land\ \forall c:\Bigl((x\leq c\land c\leq y)
        \implies\bigl((L\in\rho_4(w_c)\iff c=x)
        \land(R\in\rho_4(w_c)\iff c=y)\bigr)\Bigr).
    \end{align*}
    Note that $\delta(x,y)$ corresponds to detecting whether the sub-word $w_x\dots w_y$ corresponds to one of the words $u_i$ in the proper decomposition of $w$. We also write $\delta_2(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2)$ for
    \[
        \delta(a_1,b_1)\land\delta(a_2,b_2)\land b_1<a_2
        \land\neg\exists c:\ b_1<c<a_2,
    \]
    which similarly corresponds to identifying that $w_{a_1}\dots w_{b_1}$ and $w_{a_2}\dots w_{b_2}$ correspond to two consecutive such sub-words $u_i$ and $u_{i+1}$. 
    
    Recall that we write $(\Delta_{d-1})_{a,b}$ for $\Delta_{d-1}$ applied to the projected sub-word $\rho_1(w_a\dots w_b)$. For $s\in\{\mathrm{inc},\mathrm{dec}\}$ define
    \begin{align*}
        \Delta_{s,d}:={}&
        \forall a\forall b:\bigl(\delta(a,b)
            \implies(\Delta_{d-1})_{a,b}\bigr)\\
        &\land\ \forall a_1\forall b_1\forall a_2\forall b_2:
        \bigl(\delta_2(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2)
            \implies\psi_s(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2)\bigr).
    \end{align*}
     Finally, we define
    \begin{align*}
        \Delta_d:={}&\Gamma_d
        \land\bigl(\rho_2(w_1)=\mathrm{inc}\implies\Delta_{\mathrm{inc},d}\bigr)\\
        &\land\bigl(\rho_2(w_1)=\mathrm{dec}\implies\Delta_{\mathrm{dec},d}\bigr)\\
        &\land\bigwedge_{\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_k}
            \bigl(\rho_2(w_1)=\tau\implies\Delta_{\tau,d}\bigr).
    \end{align*}

    Given $w$ with $w\models\Gamma_d$, suppose that $w$ has profile $\tau$ and properly decomposes as  $w=u_1\dots u_\ell$. Write $\sigma_i=f_{d-1}(\rho_1(u_i))$, and we choose $\tau'$ so that $\tau' = \tau$ when $\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_k$, and otherwise $\tau'$ is the monotone permutations of length $\ell$ whose direction is given by $\tau$. 
    \begin{claim}\label{claim: central for bijection}
        We have $w\models\Delta_d$ if and only if 
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item for every $i$ we have $\rho_1(u_i)\models\Delta_{d-1}$,
            \item the expression $\tau'[\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_\ell]$ is the left-greedy decomposition of the respective permutation, and
        \item $\tau\neq \mathrm{dec}$ when $\ell=1$.
        \end{enumerate} 
    \end{claim}
    \begin{proof}
        For $\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_k$ the statement follows immediately from Lemma~\ref{lemma: handling Q_ks for bijection}. For $\tau=\mathrm{inc}$, the second line of $\Delta_{\mathrm{inc},d}$ ensures that for every $i$, we cannot write $\sigma_i \oplus \sigma_{i+1} = \theta_1 \oplus \theta_2$ with $|\theta_1| > |\sigma_i|$ (with all these permutations contained in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{k}^{[d-1]}$), and thus Lemma~\ref{lemma: albert left greedy} ensures that the expression given in the second condition indeed corresponds to the left-greedy decomposition. Finally, the first line of $\Delta_{\mathrm{inc},d}$ ensures that for each $i$, the sub-word $u_i$ is uniquely determined for the given unique $\sigma_i$. An analogous argument applies when $\tau= \mathrm{dec}$; in this case the third condition follows from the last line of $\Gamma_d$.
    \end{proof}
    \noindent Claim~\ref{claim: central for bijection} implies the uniqueness and existence of $w \in \Sigma_d^*$ with $w \models \Delta_d$ and $f_d(w) = \sigma$ for any $\sigma \in \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_k^{[d]}$. Set $L_{d} = \{w \in \Sigma_{d}^*: w \models \Delta_{d}\}$. This language is regular by Theorem~\ref{thm: closure for regular languages}, and Theorem~\ref{thm: FO correspondence} gives the required logical correspondences for the restriction of $f_{d}$ to $L_{d}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For the base case $d = 1$, we note that $v = a_{\mathrm{inc}}$ is the unique such letter. For the inductive step, suppose that $g_d(v) 
eq \star$. Note that $	au:= ho_2(v) \in \mathcal{Q}_k$ is impossible, as then $v$ (viewed as a word) must contain a letter with $ho_3$-value $i$ for each $1 \leq i \leq |	au|$. This is clearly impossible as $|	au| \geq 2$ as $v$ consists of just a single letter. If $ho_2(v) = \mathrm{dec}$, then $v$ viewed as a word must contain at least $2$ distinct positions whose $ho_4$-image contains $L$, which is again impossible.
     
     Finally, if $ho_2(v) = \mathrm{inc}$, we must have $ho_4(v) =\{L,R\}$. Thus $g_d(v) 
eq \star$ if and only if $g_{d-1}(ho_1(v)) 
eq \star $ by the construction of $g_d$. Thus $ho_1(v)$ is uniquely determined, and given that $ho_2(v) = \mathrm{inc}$ and $ho_4(v) = \{L,R\}$, the letter $v$ itself is uniquely determined.

When $d \geq 2$, the inductive structure ensures that every $w$ accepted by the automaton must decompose properly. If the type of $w$ coincides with $\tau$, the statement follows easily: note that each sub-word $u_i$ must be non-empty as the states in $B_{\tau,i}$ have only directed edges to states in $B_{\tau,j}$ with $j \in \{i,i+1\}$, and in both of these cases these  edges are labelled with letters $v$ satisfying $\rho_3(v) = j$. \begin{enumerate}

    \item the only letter in $u_i$ whose $\rho_4$-image contains $L$ is its left end-point, and the only letter in $u_i$ whose $\rho_4$-image contains $R$ is its right end-point. 
\end{enumerate}
In addition, the block $H_{\mathrm{dec}}^*$ guarantees that we must have $s \geq 2$ when the type of $w$ is $\mathrm{dec}$. This completes the proof.

label: lemma: iterative sequence lemma
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lemma: iterative sequence lemma}
    Let $C$ be a strongly connected set of states in $Q'_d$ which is located along some directed walk from the initial state to an accepting state, and which   either contain at least $2$ states or a self-loop. Then there exists an iterative sequence $\underline{\tau}$ of depth $j$ so that $C \subseteq H_{\underline{\tau}}$ and $C \not \subseteq H_{\underline{\tau},\emptyset}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the statement by induction on $d$. When $d = 1$, the only strongly connected sets $C$ satisfying the conditions are $\{q_{\mathrm{inc}}\}$ and $\{q_{\mathrm{dec}}\}$, and both clearly satisfy the statement of the Lemma.
    
    Since $C$ either contains a self-loop or at least $2$ states, it must  contain a directed cycle. Note that a simple inductive argument proves that any directed edge in $\mathcal{A}_d$ which does not end at $\star$ is labelled with a unique letter. 
    
    Let $v$ be letter attached as a label of an edge in $C$, and let $\tau = \rho_2(v)$. First consider the case when $\tau \in \mathcal{Q}_k$. Then $C$ must be clearly contained in $H_{\tau}$. Furthermore, since all the directed edges whose starting point is in $B_{\tau,i}$ have their end-point  in $B_{\tau,i} \cup B_{\tau,i+1}$, we conclude that all the states in $C$ must belong to a single $B_{\tau,i}$. Since $B_{\tau,i}$  corresponds to a copy of $Q'_{d-1}$, the inductive hypothesis implies that there exists an $\underline{\tau}' =(\tau_s,i_s)_{s = j}^{d-1}$ satisfying the conclusion of the Lemma. Thus we may choose $\underline{\tau}$ to be the sequence obtained by appending the sequence $\underline{\tau}'$ by $(\tau,i)$. 

    Now suppose that $\tau = \mathrm{inc}$. Since all the directed edges whose starting point is in $H_{\mathrm{inc}}$ have their end-point in $H_{\mathrm{inc}}\cup \{\star\}$, we conclude that $C \subseteq H_{\mathrm{inc}}$. If $C \subseteq B_{\mathrm{inc},\emptyset}$, we may apply the inductive hypothesis as above to complete the proof (and by setting $\tau_d = \mathrm{inc}$). If $C \not \subseteq B_{\mathrm{inc},\emptyset}$, we may simply choose $j = d$ and $\tau_d = \mathrm{inc}$. An analogous argument applies when $\tau = \mathrm{dec}$ and $C \subseteq H_{\mathrm{dec}}$. 
    
    Finally, suppose that $C \subseteq H_{\mathrm{dec}}^*$. Recall that all the directed edges whose starting point is in $B_{\mathrm{dec},\{R\}}^*$ or $B_{\mathrm{dec},\{L,R\}}^*$ have their end-point in $H_{\mathrm{dec}}$. Similarly, all the directed edges whose end-point is in $B_{\mathrm{dec},\{L\}}^*$ must have $e_d$ as their starting point - and note that $e_d$ is not contained in any directed cycle. Thus $C$ cannot contain vertices from any of these sets, and thus we must have $C \subseteq B_{\mathrm{dec},\emptyset}^*$. Thus we may set $\tau_d = \mathrm{dec}^*$, and again an analogous argument completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $w$, $c_1$ and $c_2$ are chosen so that $w \models \Gamma_M$ and $w \models \xi_{1,M}(c_1,c_2)$. Note that the condition $\alpha_{w,M}(c_1) \leq_1 \alpha_{w,M}(c_2)$ is trivially equivalent to the condition $\beta_{w,M}(c_1) \leq_1 \beta_{w,M}(c_2)$. 

    First consider the case when the formula on the first line is satisfied for $x = c_1, y= c_2$ and for some $(a_1,b_1)$ and $(a_2,b_2) \in \mathcal{S}$. Using observation~\eqref{eq: important observation construction beta}, $\beta_{w,M}(c_1)$ belongs to the $a_1$-th column and $\beta_{w,M}(c_2)$ belongs to the $a_2$-th column of the gridded permutation $g_M(w)$. Since $a_1 < a_2$, we must have $\beta_{w,M}(c_1) \leq_1 \beta_{w,M}(c_2)$, as required. 

    We now consider the case when the formula on the second line is satisfied for some $(a_1,b_1)$ and $(a_2,b_2)$, and write $a_* = a_1 = a_2$. Thus, the points $\beta_{w,M}(c_1)$ and $\beta_{w,M}(c_2)$ belong to the same column of $g_M(w)$, whose index we denote by $a_*$, and every non-zero entry in the column is a $\pm 1$-entry. First suppose that $\delta_{a_*} = 1$. Since $w \models \delta_{=,a_1}(c_1,c_2)$, it follows that $c_1 \leq c_2$. By the construction of the function $g_M$, this is clearly equivalent to $\beta_{w,M}(c_1) \leq_1 \beta_{w,M}(c_2)$. The case $\delta_{a_*} = -1$ follows analogously from the construction of the formula $\delta_{=,a_*}(x,y)$. 

    Finally, we consider the case when the formula on the last line is satisfied for some $(a',b')$. Thus the points $\beta_{w,M}(c_1)$ and $\beta_{w,M}(c_2)$ belong to the same cell $C_{a',b'}$ of $g_M(w)$, which is indexed by a $\star$-entry, and which contains the permutation $f_{d}(\rho_5(u_{(a',b')}))$. Since $w \models \xi_{1,d,(a',b')}(c_1,c_2)$, Lemma~\ref{lemma: inductive step of leq_1 correspondence} implies that $\beta_{w,M}(c_1) \leq_1 \beta_{w,M}(c_2)$, as required. The proof of the converse direction and the proof for $\xi_{2,M}$ follow analogously.

Write $u(a,b)$ as a shorthand for the statement that is true if and only if the letters $a$ and $b$ are unrelated. Recall that $\mathcal{S}_\pm$ denotes the indexes of the $\pm 1$ entries of $M$. For simplicity, for variables $x$, $y$ and $z$ we write $x' = \rho_6(w_x)$, $y' = \rho_6(w_y)$ and $z' = \rho_6(w_z)$. Let $\eta$ denote the first-order sentence
\[
\neg \exists x \exists y \left(x' \in \mathcal{S}_\pm \land y' \in \mathcal{S}_\pm \land x < y \land x' >_{lex} y'\land \forall z\left(x \leq z < y \implies u\left(w_z,w_y\right)\right) \right).
\]
It is easy to check that $\eta$ matches the condition of Lemma~\ref{lemma: no stars preimages given by equivalence relation}.

Let $\Delta_{M,\#}$ be the first-order sentence defined by 
\begin{align*}
\Delta_{M,\#} = \Gamma_M \land \eta \land \bigwedge_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_\star}
\left(
\left(\exists x\colon \rho_6(w_x)=(i,j)\right)
\implies (\Delta_d)_{(i,j)}
\right).
\end{align*}
It is easy to check that $\Delta_{M,\#}$  satisfies the required properties. Indeed, $\eta$ (and $\Gamma_M$) ensure that whenever $u_0$ is non-empty, the word $u_0$ corresponds to the unique representative word in the trace monoid by Lemma~\ref{lemma: no stars preimages given by equivalence relation}. 

For each $(i,j) \in \mathcal{S}_\star$, if the respective permutation in $C_{i,j}$ is non-empty, then it has a unique left-greedy representative by Theorem~\ref{thm:Main O_K}. Thus the second line ensures that either the respective sub-word $u_{(i,j)}$ is empty, or is the unique word which satisfies $\Delta_d$ and whose image coincides with $(\sigma_\#)_{i,j}$. This completes the proof.

Given variables $x_{(i,j),u,v}$ for $(i,j) \in A$ and $u,v\in \{1,2\}$, write $(\upsilon_{d,k})_{i,j}$ for the first-order formula $\upsilon_{d,k}(x_{(i,j),1,1},x_{(i,j),2,1},x_{(i,j),1,2},x_{(i,j),2,2})$, which can be used to check whether the sub-permutation induced by the points in the  rectangle $[x_{(i,j),1,1},x_{(i,j),1,2}]_1\times[x_{(i,j),2,1},x_{(i,j),2,2}]_2$ is contained in $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_k^{[d]}$. Let $\psi_A(x_{(i,j),u,v})$ denote the first-order formula
    \begin{align*}
        & \forall p: \left(\bigvee_{(i,j) \in A} \left(p \in [x_{(i,j),1,1}, x_{(i,j),1,2}]_1 \times [x_{(i,j),2,1}, x_{(i,j),2,2}]_2\right)\right) \\
        & \land \left(\bigwedge_{(i,j) \in A, u,v\in \{1,2\}} \left(x_{(i,j),u,v} \in [x_{(i,j),1,1}, x_{(i,j),1,2}]_1 \times [x_{(i,j),2,1}, x_{(i,j),2,2}]_2\right)\right) \\
        & \land \bigwedge_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{S}_\star \cap A} (\upsilon_{d,k})_{i,j} \\
        & \land \bigwedge_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{S}_+ \cap A} \left(\forall p\forall q: \left(p,q \in [x_{(i,j),1,1}, x_{(i,j),1,2}]_1 \times [x_{(i,j),2,1}, x_{(i,j),2,2}]_2 \right) \implies (p \leq_1 q \iff p  \leq_2 q)\right)\\
        & \land \bigwedge_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{S}_- \cap A} \left(\forall p\forall q: \left(p,q \in [x_{(i,j),1,1}, x_{(i,j),1,2}]_1 \times [x_{(i,j),2,1}, x_{(i,j),2,2}]_2 \right) \implies (p \leq_1 q \iff q  \leq_2 p)\right)\\
        & \land \bigwedge_{(i,j),(i',j') \in A} \left(i < i' \implies x_{(i,j),1,2} <_1 x_{(i',j'),1,1}\right) \\
        & \land \bigwedge_{(i,j),(i',j') \in A} \left(j < j' \implies x_{(i,j),2,2} <_2 x_{(i',j'),2,1}\right).
    \end{align*}
    Here, we use shorthand $p,q \in [x,y]_1\times [z,w]_2$ for the formula $(p \in [x,y]_1 \times [z,w]_2) \land (q \in [x,y]_1 \times [z,w]_2)$. 
    In order to check that $\psi_A$ satisfies the required properties, suppose that $\sigma \models \psi_{A}(c_{(i,j),u,v})$. For each $(i,j) \in A$, let $\theta_{i,j}$ denote the set of points $p \in [c_{(i,j),1,1}, c_{(i,j),1,2}]_1 \times [c_{(i,j),2,1}, c_{(i,j),2,2}]_2$. Note that at this stage we have not verified that $\theta_{i,j}$'s are disjoint nor that they are sub-intervals of $\sigma$.

    The first line implies that every $p$ belongs to at least one $\theta_{i,j}$, and the second line implies that $c_{(i,j),u,v}$'s are the smallest and largest points in $\theta_{i,j}$ under both orders respectively. In addition, the last two lines imply that whenever $i < i'$, every point $p \in \theta_{i,j}$ and every point $p' \in \theta_{i',j'}$ satisfy the condition $p <_1 p'$, and an analogous condition holds for the $\leq_2$-order whenever $j < j'$. In particular, every point $p$ belongs to exactly one $\theta_{i,j}$. 

    The third line implies that $\theta_{i,j} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_k^{[d]}$ for each $(i,j)$ with $M_{i,j} = \star$, and the fourth and fifth lines imply that the points in $\theta_{i,j}$'s with $M_{i,j} \in \{\pm 1\}$ form a monotone sub-permutation of correct direction. As these points are only guaranteed to form a monotone sub-permutation, but they do not necessarily lie on the main diagonal, it follows that there exists $\sigma_{\#} \in \mathrm{Grid}^\#(M)_{d,k}$ which satisfies the conditions of the Lemma.  To complete the proof, recall the result of Albert et. al. \cite{albert2013geometric} (stated earlier as Proposition~\ref{prop: equality grid and geometric grid when HM is a forest}), which states that $\mathrm{Grid}^\#(M)_{d,k} = \mathrm{Geom}^\#(M)_{d,k}$ whenever $M$ is a forest, and thus applies to $M_{\pm 1}$. Thus we may insert the points in the monotone cells on appropriate diagonals, which completes the proof. The proof of the converse direction follows analogously, we omit the details.

label: lemma: directed edge creates self-loop
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lemma: directed edge creates self-loop}
    $\mathcal{A}_{\pm}$ accepts exactly those words $w$ which correspond to the lexicographically minimal words. In addition, whenever $\delta_{\pm}(q_A,v) = q_B$, then $\delta_\pm(q_B,v) = q_B$. Thus every strongly connected component with at least two states contains a vertex with a self-loop.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there exists $w = w_1\dots w_\ell$ of minimal length that is lexicographically minimal, and for which $w$ is rejected by $\mathcal{A}_\pm$. Note that every proper prefix of $w$ must also be lexicographically minimal, and hence each proper prefix of $w$ is accepted by $\mathcal{A}_\pm$ by the minimality of $w$. For each $0 \leq i \leq \ell-1$, let $P_i$ denote the set chosen so that $q_{P_i} = \delta_{\pm}(q_\emptyset ,w_1\dots w_{i})$ with the convention that $P_0 = \emptyset$. Since $w$ is rejected, we have $w_\ell \in P_{\ell-1}$. 
    
    Note that for each $1 \leq i \leq \ell-1$, we have $w_\ell \in P_{i}\setminus P_{i-1}$ only when  $w_\ell \in U(w_i)$ and $w_\ell < w_i$. Let $j$ be the largest index for which we have $w_\ell \in U(w_j)$ and $w_\ell < w_j$. Thus $w_\ell$ must be contained in each of the sets $P_j,\dots,P_{\ell-1}$, and thus we must have $w_\ell \in U(w_i)$ for every $j \leq i \leq \ell-1$. However, this contradicts the third condition of Lemma~\ref{lemma: no stars preimages given by equivalence relation}. 

    Conversely, suppose that $w$ is accepted, and define $P_i$ as above for all the prefixes of $w$. If $w$ were not lexicographically minimal, then  by Lemma~\ref{lemma: no stars preimages given by equivalence relation} there exists indices $j<t$ with $w_t < w_j$ and $w_t \in U(w_i)$ for every $j \leq i < t$. Thus by the transition rules of $\mathcal{A}_\pm$ we conclude that $w_t \in P_{t-1}$, which contradicts the fact that $\mathcal{A}_\pm$ accepts $w$. Thus $w$ must be lexicographically minimal.

    Finally, suppose that $A$, $B$ and $v$ are chosen so that $\delta_\pm(q_A,v) = q_B$. Then 
    \[B= (A \cap U(v)) \cup \{c \in U(v): c < v\},\]
    and thus in particular we have $B \subseteq U(v)$. Note that we also have $v \not \in B$: indeed, as $v \not \in A$ we have $v \not \in A \cap U(v)$, and clearly $v$ is not lexicographically strictly smaller than $v$ itself, so $v$ is not contained in the second set either. 

    Let $B' = (B \cap U(v)) \cup \{c \in U(v): c < v\}$. Since $B \subseteq U(v)$ and $\{c \in U(v): c < v\} \subseteq B$, we conclude that $B' = B$. Thus, the rules of the transition function imply that $\delta_\pm(q_B,v) = q_B$. Since every strongly connected component with at least two states contains a directed edge, the existence of a vertex with a self-loop follows immediately.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows a similar idea to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma: first spectral drops lemma}. Let $C$ be the strongly connected component of $\mathcal{A}$ containing the projection of $D$, and put $\lambda = \rho(A_C)$. Since $D$ contains at least one directed edge, it follows that $C$ also contains at least  one directed edge, and hence $A_C$ is irreducible. Thus Perron-Frobenius (Theorem~\ref{thm: Perron frobenius irreducible}) gives a right eigenvector $v$ associated with $\lambda$ whose all entries are positive. 

    Write $A$ for the transition matrix of the automaton $\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{B}$, and note that $(A_D)_{(p,r),(p',r')} = A_{(p,r),(p',r')}$ for every $(p,r),(p',r') \in D$ Define a vector $v' \in \mathbb{R}^D$ by setting $v'_{(p,r)} = v_{p}$ for each $(p,r) \in D$. Note that for any $(p,r) \in D$ and $p' \in C$ we have 
    \begin{align} \label{eq:projection sum}
        \sum_{r': (p',r') \in D} (A_D)_{(p,r),(p',r')} \leq \sum_{r' \in \mathcal{B}} A_{(p,r),(p',r')} = (A_C)_{(p,p')},
    \end{align}
    as there are exactly $(A_C)_{p,p'}$ possible transitions from the state $p$ to state $p'$ in $\mathcal{A}$, and thus fixing the initial state $r \in \mathcal{B}$ while allowing the final $r'$ to be arbitrary does not restrict the choice.

    Thus for every $(p,r) \in D$ we have 
    \begin{align} \label{eq: coordwise comparison}
        (A_Dv')_{(p,r)} = \sum_{(p',r') \in D }  (A_D)_{(p,r),(p',r')} \cdot v'_{(p',r')} \leq \sum_{p' \in C} \left(v_{p'} \cdot \sum_{r' \in \mathcal{B}} A_{(p,r),(p',r')} \right)
    \end{align}
    \begin{align*}
        = \sum_{p' \in C} v_{p'} \cdot (A_C)_{p,p'} = (A_C v)_p = \lambda \cdot v_p = \lambda \cdot v'_{(p,r)},
    \end{align*}
    where the inequality between the first and second line follows from~\eqref{eq:projection sum}, and throughout the inequalities we are using the fact that all the entries of the respective matrices are non-negative, and all the entries of the vector $v$ are positive. 

    Let $w$ be the left eigenvector of $A_D$ corresponding to the  eigenvalue $\mu = \rho(A_D)$, i.e.\ $w^T A_D = \mu w^T$, and recall that all the entries of $w$ can be chosen to be positive. Then 
    \begin{align}\label{eq: between evalues}
        \mu \cdot w^T v' = w^T A_D v' = \sum_{(p,r) \in D} w_{(p,r)} \cdot (A_Dv')_{(p,r)} \leq \sum_{(p,r) \in D} w_{(p,r)} \cdot (\lambda \cdot v'_{(p,r)}) = \lambda \cdot w^T v',
    \end{align}
    where the inequality follows from inequality~\eqref{eq: coordwise comparison} and the fact that all the coordinates of $w$ and $A_Dv'$ are non-negative. In particular, we conclude that $\mu \leq \lambda$. 

    Now suppose that $\mu = \lambda$. Since each coordinate of both $v'$ and $w$ is strictly positive, it follows that inequality~\eqref{eq: coordwise comparison} is in fact equality for every $(p,r) \in D$, and hence in turn we conclude that the inequality~\eqref{eq:projection sum} must be equality for every $(p,r) \in D$ and for every $p' \in C$. In particular, every labelled directed edge in $C$ must lift to a labelled directed edge in $D$, as omitting such an edge would make the corresponding sum strictly decrease. Since $C$ is a strongly connected component, we conclude that the projection of $D$ must equal $C$.  
    
    We now prove that $D$ must be aperiodic whenever $C$ is. Suppose that $p_1,\dots,p_l$ are vertices of a closed walk of length $l$ in $C$. We claim that this lifts to a closed walk of length $l$ in $D$. Let $w = v_1\dots v_l$  denote a word which witnesses the closed walk $p_1,\dots,p_l$ with respect to $\mathcal{A}$, i.e.\ chosen so that $p_i = \delta_{\mathcal{A}}(p_1,v_1\dots v_{i-1})$ for every $2 \leq i \leq l+1$ (with $p_{l+1} = p_1$). Since $\mathcal{B}$ satisfies the condition~\eqref{eq: iterate}, it follows that there exists $N$ so that 
    $\delta_{\mathcal B}(r,w^N) = \delta_{\mathcal B}(r,w^{N+1})$ for every $r$.

    Choose $r_1'$ arbitrarily so that $(p_1,r_1') \in D$, and let $r_1,\dots,r_l$ be chosen so that $r_1 = \delta_{\mathcal{B}}(r_1',w^N)$ and $r_i = \delta_{\mathcal{B}}(r_1',w^Nv_1\dots v_{i-1})$ for every $2 \leq i \leq l$. Since
    \[
    \delta_{\mathcal{A}\times \mathcal{B}} \left((p_i,r_i), v_i\right) = (p_{i+1},r_{i+1})
    \]
    holds trivially for $1 \leq i \leq l-1$ by construction, and 
    \[\delta_{\mathcal{B}}(r_{l},v_l) = \delta_{\mathcal{B}}(r_1,w) = \delta_{\mathcal{B}}(r_1',w^{N+1}) = \delta_{\mathcal{B}}(r_1',w^N) = r_1,\]
    it follows that $\delta_{\mathcal{A}\times \mathcal{B}} \left((p_l,r_l), v_l\right) = (p_1,r_1)$. Furthermore, as all the relevant inequalities~\eqref{eq: coordwise comparison} and~\eqref{eq:projection sum} must hold with equality, we conclude that all of these points are contained in $D$. Hence $D$ contains a closed walk of length $l$. Since the same conclusion holds for all the closed walks in $C$, we conclude that $D$ must be aperiodic as well.

The statement follows immediately from this lemma if $C$ contains a directed walk of length $N$ whose edges are labelled with the same fixed letter $v$. Thus assume that such a directed walk does not exist for any $v$. Since $C$ is dominant, it contains a directed cycle and thus at least one edge. Fix a letter $v$ for which there exists a directed edge in $C$ labelled with $v$, and consider the end-point of the longest directed walk in $C$ whose edges are labelled with $v$. Such a walk must have length at most $N$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma: too long directed paths with same label}, and thus its endpoint $q := (a,b)$ has an incoming directed edge labelled with $v$, but no outgoing directed edge labelled with $v$ inside $C$. 

    Consider automaton $C'$ whose states are the states in $C$, together with additional states $q_1',\dots,q_{N}'$, and with the following transition rules. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The transitions between states inside $C$ are inherited by $C'$. 
        \item Writing $q_0' = q$, we have $\delta_{C'}(q_i',v) = q_{i+1}'$ for every $0 \leq i \leq N-1$. 
        \item For every letter $v$ and state $p$ with $\delta_C(q,v) = p$, we set $\delta_{C'}(q_N',v) = p$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Since $q$ has no outgoing edge labelled with $v$ inside $C$, the automaton $C'$ is deterministic. It is also straightforward to check that $C'$ is strongly connected. 

    Let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the words corresponding to the labels of the closed walks that are contained in $C$, based at $q$, and which do not revisit $q$ in the middle. Note that the same directed cycle can contribute multiple words if its edges are attached with several labels. We define $\mathcal{C}'$ analogously. 

    Let $G$ and $G'$ denote the sets of all the words $u_1\dots u_s$ with $u_i \in \mathcal{C}$ or $u_i \in \mathcal{C'}$ respectively, including the empty word in both cases. Note that
    \[
    |G_n| = (A_C^n)_{q,q} \qquad\text{and}\qquad |G_n'| = (A_{C'}^n)_{q,q}.

        \begin{align} \label{eq: directed path}
            \delta_\pm(a_{i-1},w'_i) = a_i 
        \end{align}
        holds for every $1 \leq i \leq l$. Indeed, if both $p_{i-1}$ and $p_i$ are contained in $C$ then~\eqref{eq: directed path} follows from the fact that $w_i'$ is a label on the directed edge $p_{i-1} \rightarrow p_i$.

Indeed, there is an incoming edge inside $C$ to $q$ labelled with $v$, which implies that  there is an incoming edge to the state $a$ labelled with $v$ inside $\mathcal{A}_\pm$. Thus Lemma~\ref{lemma: directed edge creates self-loop} implies that the state $a$ has a self-loop labelled with $v$ in $\mathcal{A}_\pm$, which implies~\eqref{eq: directed path}. Finally, in the remaining case we must have $p_{i-1} = q_N'$, and the statement follows from the fact that the outgoing edges and their labels from $q_N'$ coincide with those of the state $q$. Thus~\eqref{eq: directed path} holds for all $1 \leq i \leq l$. In particular, $w'$ matches the labels of a closed walk in $\mathcal{A}_\pm$, and hence $w'$ is a contiguous sub-word of a lexicographically minimal word. Thus $w'$ itself must be lexicographically minimal, and hence the restriction of $g$ on $G'$ induces an injection. 

        Recall from Lemma~\ref{thm: Albert et al regular language} that the function $g$ is order-preserving, i.e.\ whenever $u$ is a sub-word of $w$, then $g(u)$ is a sub-pattern of $g(w)$ as a gridded permutation. Given $w'\in G'$, we follow its unique closed walk in $C'$. Every visit to one of the new states $q_i'$ corresponds to visiting the states $q,q_1',\dots,q_N'$ in this order. Furthermore, the final transition from $q_N'$ onward cannot be labelled with the letter $v$ as $q$ has no outgoing directed edges in $C$ with label $v$. In particular, such visit corresponds to a contiguous sub-word of the form $v^N$, and such letters must be the last $N$ instances of the letter $v$ in a contiguous sub-word of the form $v^i$ in $w'$ with $i \geq N$ (and hence we must always have $i \leq 2N-1$). 

        Given $w' \in G'$, replace each contiguous block of $v^N$ which is at the end of the word $w'$ or followed by a letter $v' \neq v$ with the word $u_0^N$, and write $w''$ for the word obtained as the outcome of this process. This completes the proof of Claim~\ref{claim: important injectivity claim}. 
    \end{proof}
    Given Claim~\ref{claim: important injectivity claim}, the result follows easily. Write $\mu = \rho(A_C)$ and $\mu' = \rho(A_{C'})$. Order the states of $C'$ so that those in $C$ occur at the first $|C|$ rows and columns in $A_{C'}$, and let $B$ denote the matrix obtained by adding $N$ zero rows and columns at the end of $A_C$. Then $A:=A_{C'}$ and $B$ satisfy the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lemma: first spectral drops lemma}, and thus $\mu<\mu'$. Hence Claim~\ref{claim: important injectivity claim} implies that 
    \[
    \mu < \mu' = \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left((A_{C'}^n)_{q,q}\right)^{1/n} \leq \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n^\#|^{1/n} = \rho(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{F},\#}).
    \]
    In particular, $C$ cannot be dominant, which gives the required contradiction.

    Now suppose that the statement holds for $d-1$, and suppose that $w$ decomposes properly as $w = u_1\dots u_\ell$. For each $1 \leq i \leq \ell$ write $\theta_i = f_{d-1}(\rho_1(u_i))$. Let $I$ be a monotone sub-interval of length $s$ in $f_d(w)$, and let $J \subseteq [\ell]$ be chosen so that $I$ has non-empty intersection with the block of $f_d(w)$ corresponding to $f_{d-1}(\rho_1(u_i))$ whenever $i \in J$. Note that $J$ is clearly a sub-interval $\{a,\dots,b\}$. For simplicity, we only consider the case when $I$ is monotone increasing. 

    If $b \geq a+2$, the block corresponding to $f_{d-1}(\rho_1(u_{a+1}))$ is fully contained in $I$, and hence $f_{d-1}(\rho_1(u_{a+1}))$ itself must be a monotone increasing permutation. Let $\tau$ be either the profile of $w$ or the increasing\footnote{Note that the profile cannot be $\mathrm{dec}$ as $I$ is monotone increasing and $b > a$.} permutation of length $\ell$. Since $w \models \Delta_d$, the left-greedy decomposition of $f_d(w)$ is given as 
    \[f_d(w) = \tau[\theta_1,\dots,\theta_\ell].\]
    Since $b \geq a+2$ and $\theta_{a+1}$ is monotone increasing, we may move the points from $I\cap \theta_{a+2}$ into $\theta_{a+1}$, and thus obtain a decomposition which is smaller with respect to the left-greedy order. This gives the desired contradiction, and implies that we must have $b \leq a+1$. 

    Now suppose that $b \in \{a,a+1\}$. Thus by the pigeonhole principle we have $|I\cap \theta_a|\geq \frac{s}{2}$ or $|I \cap \theta_{a+1}| \geq \frac{s}{2}$. Applying the inductive hypothesis with $w' = \rho_1(u_t)$  and to the interval $I' = I \cap \theta_t$, where $t$ is chosen so that $|I'| \geq \frac{s}{2} > 2^{d-2}((d-1)+k)$, it follows that $w'$ contains a contiguous constant sub-sequence of length $N':=\frac{s/2}{2^{d-2}} - 2(d-1)$.     \begin{enumerate}
        \item The transitions between states inside $C$ are inherited by $C'$. 
        \item Writing $q_0' = q_{s+4}'= q$, we have $\delta_{C'}(q_{i-1}',c_i) = q_{i}'$ for every $1 \leq i \leq s+4$. 
    \end{enumerate}
    That is, we add $s+3$ new states which form a closed cycle based at $q$ which corresponds to the word $c':= c_1\dots c_{s+4}$. Thus it is easy to see that every word $w$ accepted by $C'$ can be decomposed uniquely as 
    \begin{align}\label{eq: unique decomposition}
        w = u_1c'u_2c'\dots c'u_r,
    \end{align}
    where $u_1,\dots,u_r\in L_\mathcal{C}$, and they are allowed to be empty. Let $L_\mathcal{C'}$ denote the set of words accepted by $C'$, and define $h': L_\mathcal{C'} \rightarrow \mathfrak{S}$ by setting 
    \begin{align}\label{eq: definition of h'}
        h'(w)= h(u_1) \oplus \mu \oplus h(u_2) \oplus \mu \oplus \dots \oplus \mu \oplus h(u_r),    
    \end{align}
    where $h(\varepsilon)$ is defined to be the empty permutation. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma: aperiodicity or drops for plusminus}, the following essentially completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma: periodic drops in A_d}.  

    \begin{claim}\label{claim: important counting claim for A_d}
        The following statements are true. 
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $h'$ is a length-preserving map.
            \item $h'$ is an injection.
            \item $h'(w) \in \mathcal{F}$ for every $w \in L_{\mathcal{C'}}$. 
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{claim}
    \begin{proof}
        We note that $h'$ is clearly length-preserving by its construction. To prove that $h'$ is an injection, we note by Corollary~\ref{cor: no long monotone subintervals for hs} and by the choice of $s$, for every $w \in L_\mathcal{C'}$, any monotone sub-interval of length at least $s$ must be contained in a copy of $\mu$ in the expression of $h'(w)$ via~\eqref{eq: definition of h'}, and thus must correspond to the contiguous sub-words of $w$ that are of the form $c'$. In particular, given $\sigma = h'(w)$, we may recover each copy of $\mu$ in the decomposition~\eqref{eq: definition of h'} from monotone sub-intervals of length $s$. Deleting such copies of $\mu$ corresponds to deleting all the sub-words $c'$ from $w$. Thus injectivity of $h'$ follows from the injectivity of $h$. 

        Let $u_0 \in L_\mathcal{C}$ be chosen so that $|u_0| \geq s$. Thus $h(u_0)$ cannot be a monotone permutation, and hence it contains $21$ as a sub-permutation. Given $w \in L_\mathcal{C'}$, suppose $w$ decomposes as 
        \[w = u_1c'u_2c'\dots c'u_r,\]
        where $u_1,\dots,u_r \in L_{\mathcal{C}}$ or $u_i = \varepsilon$. Let $u' = (u_0)^{s+2}$, and define the particular word $w'$ as 
        \[w' = u_1u'u_2u' \dots u'u_r.\]
        Since each $u_0,u_1,\dots,u_r$ corresponds to a closed walk in $C$ based at $q$, we conclude that $w' \in L_\mathcal{C}$. Furthermore, we have 
        \[h(w') = h(u_1) \oplus h(u') \oplus h(u_2) \oplus \dots \oplus h(u') \oplus h(u_r). \]
        Since $u' = (u_0)^{s+2}$, we have 
        \[h(u') = h(u_0) \oplus \dots \oplus h(u_0),\]
        where the direct sum consists of $s+2$ copies of $h(u_0)$. We claim that $\mu$ is a sub-permutation of $h(u')$. Indeed, since $h(u_0)$ is not a monotone increasing permutation, it contains $21$ as a sub-permutation. Delete all but two points forming a sub-permutation $21$ from the first and last copies of $h(u_0)$, and all but one points from the middle $s$ copies of $h(u_0)$. Then the resulting permutation is 
        \[21 \oplus 1 \oplus \dots \oplus 1 \oplus 21 = 21 \oplus 12 \dots s \oplus 21 = \mu,\]
        which verifies the fact that $\mu$ is a sub-permutation of $h(u')$. Hence 
        \[h'(w) = h(u_1) \oplus \mu \oplus h(u_2) \oplus \dots \oplus \mu \oplus h(u_r)\]
        is a sub-permutation of $h(w')$. Since $w' \in L_\mathcal{C}$, Lemma~\ref{lemma: important properties of h} implies that $h(w') \in \mathcal{F}$. Since $\mathcal{F}$ is a closed under sub-patterns, we conclude that $h'(w) \in \mathcal{F}$. This completes the proof. 
    \end{proof}

    Equipped with Claim~\ref{claim: important counting claim for A_d}, the rest of the proof follows easily. Set $\lambda=\rho(A_C)$ and $\lambda'=\rho(A_{C'})$. Since $C'$ can be easily checked to be strongly connected, it follows that the matrix $A_{C'}$ is irreducible. Let $B$ denote the matrix obtained by adding $|C'| - |C|$ rows and columns consisting of $0$'s to the matrix $A_C$. Then $A_{C'}$ and $B$ satisfy the conditions  of Lemma~\ref{lemma: first spectral drops lemma}, and hence we must have $\lambda'>\lambda$. Since $C$ is dominant, we have 
    \[\lambda = \rho(A_C) = \rho(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{F},\#}) = \limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n^\#|^{1/n}.\]
    
    Since Claim~\ref{claim: important counting claim for A_d} implies that we have $h'(w) \in \mathcal{F}$ for every $w \in L_{\mathcal{C'}}$, we conclude that 
    \[
        (A_{C'}^n)_{q,q}\leq |\mathcal F_n|\leq |\mathcal F_n^\#|,
    \]
    and thus 
    \[\lambda' = \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty}((A_{C'}^n)_{q,q})^{1/n} \leq \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty}|\mathcal F_n^\#|^{1/n} = \lambda.\]
    This contradicts the fact that $\lambda' > \lambda$, and completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $A$ for the transition matrix of $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{F},\#}$ once the non-productive states have been removed, and write $A'$ for the transition matrix of $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{F}$ once the non-productive states have been removed. Write $\mu = \rho(A)$ and $\mu' = \rho(A')$, and recall that we have $\mu = \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n^\#|^{1/n}$ and $\mu' = \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n|^{1/n}$. As Lemma~\ref{lemma: gridded of by poly factor} implies that 
\begin{align*}
    \limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n|^{1/n} &\leq \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n^\#|^{1/n} \leq \limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty} \left(\binom{n+l}{l}\cdot \binom{n+m}{m}\cdot |\mathcal{F}_n| \right)^{1/n} = \limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n|^{1/n},
\end{align*}
we conclude that 
\[\mu' = \limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n|^{1/n} = \limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty} |\mathcal{F}_n^\#|^{1/n} = \mu.\]

Let $C$ denote a dominant component in $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{F}$, and let $D$ denote the strongly connected component in $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{F},\#}$ containing the projection of $C$. Then Lemma~\ref{lemma: loose radius or maintain aperiodicity} implies that $\rho(A'_C) \leq \rho(A_D)$, and hence
\[\mu = \rho(A'_C) \leq \rho(A_D) \leq \rho(A) = \mu.\]
Thus we must have $\rho(A'_C) = \rho(A_D) = \mu$, and hence $D$ is a dominant component in $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{F},\#}$. Thus $D$ is aperiodic either by Lemma~\ref{lemma: aperiodicity or drops for plusminus} or by Lemma~\ref{lemma: periodic drops in A_d}. Hence Lemma~\ref{lemma: loose radius or maintain aperiodicity} implies that $C$ must be aperiodic as well, which completes the proof.

title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a small permutation class. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Then there exists a regular language $L_{\mathcal{F}}$ and a length-preserving bijection
        \[f_{\mathcal{F}}: L_{\mathcal{F}} \rightarrow \mathcal{F}\]
        satisfying the following property: for every first-order logic sentence $\Psi$ on $\mathcal{F}$ there exists a first-order logic  sentence $\Phi$ on $L_{\mathcal{F}}$ so that 
        \[\{w \in L_\mathcal{F}: w \models \Phi\} = \{w \in L_\mathcal{F}: f_\mathcal{F}(w) \models \Psi\}.\]
        The same conclusion also holds for sentences in monadic second-order logic.
        \item{(sketched)} The bijection $f_\mathcal{F}$ is in fact a monadic second-order isomorphism: that is, for every sentence $\Phi$ in monadic second-order logic on $L_\mathcal{F}$ there exists a corresponding sentence in monadic second-order logic on $\mathcal{F}$ for which the conclusion above holds. In addition, it is also possible to construct a regular language $L_\mathcal{F}'$ and a length-preserving bijection $f'_\mathcal{F}: L_\mathcal{F}' \rightarrow \mathcal{F}$ which is a first-order isomorphism. 
        \item For the last three assertions, suppose that $\mathcal{F}$ is not finite. There exist a positive real number $\alpha$, a real number $\beta \geq 1$, and a non-negative integer $c$ so that 
        \[\vert \mathcal{F}_n\vert = (\alpha+o(1))\cdot \beta ^n\cdot n^c.\]
        \item Given a monadic second-order sentence $\Psi$ on $\mathcal{F}$, write \[\mathcal{F}^\Psi_n := \{\sigma \in \mathcal{F}_n: \sigma \models \Psi\}.\]
        Then the sets $\mathcal{F}^\Psi_n$ have a rational generating function.
        \item For every first-order $\mathrm{TOTO}$ sentence $\Phi$ the limit  $\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \mathbb{P} (\pi \models \Phi)$ exists, where $\pi$  is taken uniformly at random from $\mathcal{F}_n$. 
    \end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $d$ and $k$ be positive integers and let $M$ be a multiplicative $\star$-isolated forest matrix chosen so that $\mathcal{F} \subseteq \mathrm{Geom}(M)_{d,k}$. Note that such $M$ exists by Proposition~\ref{prop: small implies contained inside Geom (M) dk}. Since $\mathcal{F}$ is a small permutation class, Proposition~\ref{prop: small classes FOS classifiable} implies that there exists a first-order sentence $\hat{\upsilon}_{\mathcal{F}}$ so that $\sigma \models \hat{\upsilon}_\mathcal{F}$ if and only if $\sigma \in \mathcal{F}$. 

    Let $\chi_{\mathcal{F}}$ be the first-order sentence in $\Sigma_M^*$ obtained by applying Theorem~\ref{thm: FO correspondence for M} to the sentence $\hat{\upsilon}_{\mathcal{F}}$, and set $L_{\mathcal{F}} = \{w \in \Sigma_M^*: w \models \Delta_M \land \chi_{\mathcal{F}}\}$. Thus Theorem~\ref{thm: closure for regular languages} implies that $L_{\mathcal{F}}$ is a regular language, and Theorem~\ref{thm: FO correspondence for M} implies that the restriction $f_\mathcal{F}$ of $f_M$ on $L_{\mathcal{F}}$ is both a first-order and a monadic second-order homomorphism. Finally, since the restriction of $f_M$ on $\{w\in \Sigma_M^*: w\models \Delta_M\}$ induces a bijection whose image is $\mathrm{Geom}(M)_{d,k}$, it follows that $f_\mathcal{F}$ induces a bijection from $L_{\mathcal{F}}$ to $\mathcal{F}$. This completes the proof of the first part. 
    
     Let $\mathcal{A'}_\mathcal{F}$ denote the automaton obtained by removing the unproductive states from the automaton $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{F}$ constructed in Theorem~\ref{thm: automata main theorem}. Thus by Theorem~\ref{thm: automata main theorem} all the dominant strongly connected components of $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{F}$ are aperiodic, and at least one such component must exist as $\mathcal{F}$ is not finite. Hence Lemma~\ref{lemma: primitive dominant asymptotics} implies that there exists positive constant $c$, non-negative integer $k$ and $\lambda \geq 1$ so that 
    \[a_n:=|\mathcal{F}_n| = (c+o(1))\cdot \lambda^n \cdot n^k\]
    as $n\rightarrow \infty$. This completes the proof of the third part. 
    
    Let $\Psi$ be a monadic second-order sentence on $\mathcal{F}$, and let $\Phi$ denote the first-order sentence on words for which we have 
    \[\{w\in L_{\mathcal{F}}:w\models \Phi\}=\{w \in L_\mathcal{F}:f_{\mathcal{F}}(w) \models \Psi\}.\]
    Define $L_\mathcal{F}^\Phi := \{w \in L_{\mathcal{F}}: w\models \Phi\}$. Then $L_\mathcal{F}^\Phi$ is a monadic second-order restriction of a regular language, and thus itself a regular language by Theorem~\ref{thm: closure for regular languages}.  Hence the sets $(L_\mathcal{F}^\Phi)_n$ has a rational generating function by Theorem~\ref{thm: reg languages have RGF}, and thus $\mathcal{F}^\Psi_n$ also have rational generating function, which completes the proof of the fourth part. 
    
    Let $\Psi$ be a first-order sentence on permutations, and again we write $\Phi$ for the corresponding first-order sentence on words. Let $\mathcal{B}_\Phi$ denote the automaton chosen to satisfy the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lemma: iterate}, and set $\mathcal{A}_\Psi := \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{F} \times B_\Phi$. Then $\mathcal{A}_\Psi$ accepts precisely those $w \in L_{\mathcal{F}}$ with $w \models \Phi$. 

    Define $b_n = |\mathcal{F}_n^\Psi|$. If $b_n = 0$ for sufficiently large $n$, then the limit is clearly $0$. Otherwise, let $\mathcal{A}_\Psi'$ denote the automaton obtained from $\mathcal{A}_\Psi$ by removing all the unproductive states. Then $\mathcal{A}_\Psi'$ accepts the same words as $\mathcal{A}_\Psi$, and since it accepts infinitely many words, it contains at least one directed cycle. 
    
    Let $\mu$ denote the largest spectral radius of a strongly connected component in $\mathcal{A}_\Psi'$, and let $r+1$ denote the largest number of strongly connected components with spectral radius $\mu$ along any walk from the initial state to an accepting state. Then standard properties of regular languages imply that $|\mathcal{F}_n^\Psi| \leq  C\cdot n^{r}\mu^n$ for some constant $C$. 

    If $\mu < \lambda$, then 
    \[\limsup_{n\rightarrow  \infty} \mathbb{P}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma_n} \in \mathcal{F}_n: \boldsymbol{\sigma_n} \models \Psi\right) = \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{b_n}{a_n} \leq \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \frac{C\cdot n^r \cdot \mu^n}{c\cdot n^k \cdot \lambda^n} = 0,\] 
    and thus in particular the limit exists. If $\mu \geq \lambda$, let $C$ be a strongly connected component in $\mathcal{A}_\Psi'$ with spectral radius $\mu$, and let $D$ be the strongly connected component in $\mathcal{A'}_{\mathcal{F}}$ containing its projection. Write $A$ and $B$ for the transition matrices of $\mathcal{A'}_\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{A}_\Psi'$ respectively. By Lemma~\ref{lemma: loose radius or maintain aperiodicity} we have $\rho(B_C) \leq \rho(A_D)$, and thus 
    \[\lambda \leq \mu = \rho(B_C) \leq \rho(A_D) \leq \lambda.\]
    Thus we must have $\rho(B_C) = \rho(A_D) = \lambda$, and hence $D$ must be a dominant component, and hence $D$ is aperiodic by Theorem~\ref{thm: automata main theorem}. Since $\rho(B_C) = \rho(A_D)$,  Lemma~\ref{lemma: loose radius or maintain aperiodicity} in turn implies that $C$ must be aperiodic. 
    
    Thus every dominant component in $\mathcal{A}_\Psi$ must be aperiodic, and thus Lemma~\ref{lemma: primitive dominant asymptotics} implies that there exits $c'>0$ for which $b_n =(c'+o(1))\cdot n^r \cdot \lambda^n$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Thus 
    \[\lim_{n\rightarrow  \infty} \mathbb{P}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma_n} \in \mathcal{F}_n: \boldsymbol{\sigma_n} \models \Psi\right) = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{b_n}{a_n} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{c'\cdot n^r}{c \cdot n^k}.\] 
    If $r = k$, the limit exists and equals $\frac{c'}{c}$. If $r < k$, the limit exists and equals $0$. Since $b_n \leq a_n$ for every $n$, we cannot have $r > k$. This completes the proof of the final part.

title: Proof
body_md:
For clarity we write $\alpha_w : = \alpha_{w,M}$. The atomic formulas are of the form $w_i = a$, $i < j$, $i = j$ and $i \in A$, where $a$ is a letter, $i$ and $j$ are first-order variables, and $A$ is a second-order variable. Again, the last two formulas are simple to translate into formulas on permutations.

    For the atomic formulas of the form $w_i =a$, we may use Lemma~\ref{lemma: left-greedy drawing, which has its extremal points in A} to write down a condition for the corresponding $p:=\alpha_w(i)$ which ensures that $p$ belongs to the cell in the left-greedy representation $\sigma_\#$ of $\sigma:=f_M(w)$ described by $(i',j'):=\rho_6(a)$. If $a \in \Sigma_{M,\pm}$, this translation on its own suffices. If $a \in \Sigma_{\star,(i',j')}$, we set $b:=\rho_5(a)$ and write down the appropriate condition inductively.

    The base case $d = 1$ is easy to handle, we omit the details. If $\rho_2(b) = \tau \in \mathcal{Q}_k$, we may use the first part of Lemma~\ref{lemma: handling Q_ks for bijection} to write down a condition which ensures that $p$ belongs to the $\rho_3(b)$-th block of $(\sigma_\#)_{(i',j')}$, and proceed by induction within this block. 
    
    If $\rho_2(b) \in \{\mathrm{inc},\mathrm{dec}\}$, we write $u_{i',j'}$ for the sub-word of $w$ consisting of letters whose $\rho_6$-projection equals $(i',j')$, and suppose that $\rho_5(u_{i',j'})$ decomposes properly as $u_1\dots u_s$. By using Lemmas ~\ref{lemma: albert left greedy} and~\ref{lemmma: oplus} it is easy to construct a second-order variable $B$ which consists of the left-most points in the left-greedy decomposition of the corresponding permutation. We may then apply the inductive hypothesis inside this block. Note that at this step we have to be slightly careful with points whose $\rho_4$ image is $\{L\}$, $\{R\}$ or $\{L,R\}$, but we may again construct a first-order sentence by induction to handle this technicality.  We remark that this is the step which does not carry over to the first-order logic: the construction of the second-order variable $B$ is required even if we apply the construction to a first-order sentence. 
    
    For atomic formulas $i < j$, we write $p = \alpha_w(i)$ and $q = \alpha_w(j)$. Note that other parts of the monadic second-order sentence must impose some conditions on the $\rho_6$-images of $w_i$ and $w_j$, which correspond to the cells of the left-greedy decomposition of $f_M(w)$ containing $p$ and $q$ respectively. Since the extremal points of the left-greedy decomposition are first-order definable, the translation is trivial if the other conditions force $p$ and $q$ to be contained in different cells. If $p$ and $q$ belong to same cell indexed by $\pm 1$-entry, we may use $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_l$ to translate the condition $i<j$ to a condition comparing $p$ and $q$ with respect to the order $<_1$. For $\star$-entries, we may simply construct such a formula by induction on $d$, we omit the details as the technique is similar to the one used above.

    \begin{align*}
         &\left(\forall z  \left(z \leq_1 x_{s,1,2} \implies \bigvee_{i=1}^{s} \left(z \in [x_{i,1,1},x_{i,1,2}]_1 \times [x_{i,2,1},x_{i,2,2}]_2\right)\right)\right) \\
         & \land \bigwedge_{i,i'=1}^{s}  \bigwedge_{u,u'=1}^{2} \bigwedge_{v,v'=1}^{2} \left(i < i' \implies \left(x_{i,u,v} <_1 x_{i',u',v'} \land x_{i,u,v} <_2 x_{i',u',v'})\right)\right) \\
         & \land \bigwedge_{i=1}^{s} \upsilon_{d-1,k}(x_{i,1,1},x_{i,2,1},x_{i,1,2},x_{i,2,2})
        \\ &\land\bigwedge_{i=1}^{s}\bigwedge_{u,v=1}^{2}
        \left(x_{i,u,v}\in
        [x_{i,1,1},x_{i,1,2}]_1\times
        [x_{i,2,1},x_{i,2,2}]_2\right)
        \\ & \land \left(\forall z_1 \forall z_2: \left(z_1 \leq_1 x_{s,1,2} \land x_{s,1,2} <_1 z_2\right) \implies z_1 <_2 z_2\right)
    \end{align*}
    Let $a_{i,u,v}$ be chosen so that $\sigma \models \psi_{\mathrm{inc},s}(a_{i,u,v})$, and for $1 \leq i \leq s$ , write $\sigma_i$ for the sub-permutation induced by the points in $[a_{i,1,1},a_{i,1,2}]_1 \times [a_{i,2,1},a_{i,2,2}]_2$. We also write $\sigma_{s+1}$ for the remaining points. Then the first and last lines imply that $\sigma = \varphi \oplus \sigma_{s+1}$, where $\varphi$ consists of the points in $\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{s}$. Analogously as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma: handling Q_ks for bijection}, we conclude that the remaining lines imply that $\varphi = \sigma_1 \oplus \dots \oplus \sigma_s$ and that for all $1 \leq i \leq s$ we have $\sigma_i \in \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_k^{[d-1]}$. 

    Analogously, we set $\psi_{\mathrm{dec},s}(x_{i,u,v})$ to be the formula 
    \begin{align*}
         &\left(\forall z  \left(z \leq_1 x_{s,1,2} \implies \bigvee_{i=1}^{s} \left(z \in [x_{i,1,1},x_{i,1,2}]_1 \times [x_{i,2,1},x_{i,2,2}]_2\right)\right)\right) \\
         & \land \bigwedge_{i,i'=1}^{s}  \bigwedge_{u,u'=1}^{2} \bigwedge_{v,v'=1}^{2} \left(i < i' \implies \left(x_{i,u,v} <_1 x_{i',u',v'} \land x_{i',u',v'} <_2 x_{i,u,v})\right)\right) \\
         & \land \bigwedge_{i=1}^{s} \upsilon_{d-1,k}(x_{i,1,1},x_{i,2,1},x_{i,1,2},x_{i,2,2})
        \\ &\land\bigwedge_{i=1}^{s}\bigwedge_{u,v=1}^{2}
        \left(x_{i,u,v}\in
        [x_{i,1,1},x_{i,1,2}]_1\times
        [x_{i,2,1},x_{i,2,2}]_2\right)
        \\ & \land \left(\forall z_1 \forall z_2: \left(z_1 \leq_1 x_{s,1,2} \land x_{s,1,2} <_1 z_2\right) \implies z_2 <_2 z_1\right),
    \end{align*}
    and we note that checking the details follows similarly.

\label{lemma: final step}
    Let $\alpha \in \{\mathrm{inc},\mathrm{dec}\}$ and let $s$ be a positive integer. Then there exists a first-order formulas $\psi'_{\alpha,s}(x_{i,u,v})$ with $i \in [s], u,v\in \{1,2\}$ so that for $\sigma \in \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{k}^{[d]}$ we have  $\sigma \models \psi'_{\alpha,s}(a_{i,u,v})$ if and only if the left-greedy decomposition of $\sigma$ is given as $\tau_r[\theta_1,\dots,\theta_r]$ for some $r \geq s+1$, where $\tau_r$ is the monotone permutation of length $r$ and direction $\alpha$, and for each $1\leq i\leq s$ the permutation $\theta_i$ consists of the points in $[a_{i,1,1},a_{i,1,2}]_1 \times [a_{i,2,1},a_{i,2,2}]_2$, and each $a_{i,u,v}$ belongs to $\theta_i$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the first-order formula $\psi'_{\mathrm{inc},s}(x_{i,u,v})$ with $i \in [s], u,v\in \{1,2\}$ given by 
    \begin{align*}
        &\bigwedge_{\tau \in \mathcal{Q}_k\cup(\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{k,s}} \left(\forall_{i \in [|\tau|]} x_i,y_i: \neg \psi_{\tau}(x_1,\dots,x_{|\tau|},y_1,\dots,y_{|\tau|})\right)
        \\& \land \neg \left(\exists z\exists u\forall x\forall y:(z <_1 u)\land \left((x \leq_1 z\land z<_1y)\implies y<_2x\right)\right)
        \\& \land \psi_{\mathrm{inc},s}(x_{i,u,v}) \land \left(\forall_{i\in [s],u,v\in \{1,2\}} y_{i,u,v}: \psi_{\mathrm{inc},s}(y_{i,u,v})\implies \bigwedge_{i=1}^s \left(y_{i,2,2} \leq_2x_{i,2,2} \right)\right).
    \end{align*}
    We check that $\psi'_{\mathrm{inc},s}$ satisfies the required properties. Suppose that $\sigma \models \psi'_{\mathrm{inc},s}(a_{i,u,v})$, and let $\sigma = \tau[\theta_1,\dots,\theta_r]$ denote the left-greedy decomposition of $\sigma$. The first line excludes every non-monotone permutation and every monotone permutation of length at most $s$ as the profile $\tau$ of $\sigma$. Thus $\tau$ must be a monotone permutation of length at least $s+1$. 

    Recall that Proposition~2.3 in~\cite{albert2015inflations} implies that for any $\sigma \in \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{k}^{[d]}$, the set $T(\sigma)$ of possible profiles $\tau'$  of decompositions of $\sigma$ as $\sigma = \tau'[\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_\ell]$ with $\sigma_i \in \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{k}^{[d-1]}$ has a unique minimum element under sub-pattern containment. 

    The second line implies that it is impossible to write down $\sigma$ as a skew-sum of two non-empty permutations. Thus, by the observation above, this condition is equivalent to the profile $\tau$ of $\sigma$ being a monotone increasing permutation, and hence a monotone increasing permutation of length at least $s+1$. 

    For each $1 \leq i\leq s$ and $u,v\in \{1,2\}$, let $b_{i,u,v}\in \theta_i$ be chosen so that $\theta_i$ consists of the points in $[b_{i,1,1},b_{i,1,2}]_1 \times [b_{i,2,1},b_{i,2,2}]_2$. Let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s$ be defined as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma: key inflation lemma}.
    
    Since $\sigma \models \psi'_{\mathrm{inc},s}$, the last line implies that for all $1 \leq j \leq s$ we have $\sum_{i=1}^j|\theta_i| \leq \sum_{i=1}^j |\sigma_i|$. If the inequality is strict for some $j$, pick the least $j$ for which it is strict. Writing $\theta_i' = \theta_i$ for $i < j$, $\theta_j' = \sigma_j$ and  $\theta_i' = \theta_i \setminus \sigma_j$ for $i \geq j+1$, we have $\sigma = \theta_1' \oplus \dots \oplus \theta_r'$, omitting the empty blocks. This gives a decomposition of $\sigma$ as a direct sum of fewer blocks, or with the same number of blocks and larger $j$-th block, thus contradicting the fact that $\theta_1 \oplus \dots \oplus \theta_r$ is the left-greedy decomposition of $\sigma$.

    Thus the equality $\sum_{i=1}^j|\theta_i| =\sum_{i=1}^j |\sigma_i|$ must hold for every $1 \leq j \leq s$. Hence we conclude that $|\theta_i| = |\sigma_i|$ and hence $\sigma_i = \theta_i$ holds for each $1 \leq i\leq s$. Hence the $i$-th block $\theta_i$ in the left-greedy decomposition consists of points $[a_{i,1,1},a_{i,1,2}]_1 \times [a_{i,2,1},a_{i,2,2}]_2$. The proof of the converse direction follows similarly, we omit the details. 

    The construction of $\psi'_{\mathrm{dec},s}(x_{i,u,v})$ follows analogously, we omit the details.
